title: SafetyPulse: Catching Safety Drift During Fine-Tuning by Reading the Model's Refusal Circuit
gist: A hackathon team shows benign LoRA fine-tuning of Cohere Labs' Tiny Aya Global raises harmful-compliance (ASR 14.3% to 25.2%), introduces a Circuit Integrity Score that flags every unsafe held-out checkpoint 1-3 checkpoints early for about USD 0.005 per check, and finds SafeTune's optimal low-rank rollback repairs both safety and lost math accuracy while circuit-only weight restoration fails.

insights.claim: Fine-tuning Cohere Labs' Tiny Aya Global (3.35B) on 2,000 harmless Alpaca instructions raised attack success rate on held-out HarmBench prompts from 14.3% to 25.2%.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Any enterprise customizing open-weight models inherits latent safety regressions even with clean data, creating liability and demand for checkpoint auditing.
insights.quote:
On Tiny Aya, 2,000
Alpaca instructions raise the attack success rate (ASR) on held-out HarmBench prompts from 14.3% to 25.2%.

insights.claim: After benign Alpaca fine-tuning, the model's over-refusal on safe XSTest prompts fell from 7.3% to 1.3%, meaning the model refuses less of everything rather than selectively losing harmful-request refusals.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Fine-tunes that look 'more helpful' on user metrics may be masking a broad safety loss.
insights.quote: the model refuses less of everything

insights.claim: Teams that adapt open-weight models to a domain or language typically skip per-checkpoint safety audits because generating and judging hundreds of harmful-prompt responses is costly, so models that refuse less get shipped.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Points to an underserved market for cheap, automated safety QA in the fine-tuning pipeline.
insights.quote:
Catching the erosion means
auditing every checkpoint, generating answers to hundreds of harmful prompts and judging them, so it is usually
skipped, and a model that refuses less gets shipped.

insights.claim: Data curation with CuratorKIT (schema, deduplication, secrets and toxicity gates) removed only 19 of 2,000 Alpaca examples, and a fine-tune on the cleaned data drifted just the same (mean ASR 37.6% vs 38.1%), indicating drift comes from ordinary instruction tuning rather than toxic data.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Data-hygiene vendors cannot sell curation as a safety guarantee; monitoring is a separate necessary layer.
insights.quote:
data
hygiene is no substitute for monitoring.
insights.locator: 6.6 Does curating the data prevent the drift?

insights.claim: Fine-tuning Tiny Aya Global on GSM8K math data, and on a negative-control mix of 1,800 Alpaca instructions plus 200 refusals, left the model slightly safer, so safety drift depends on the type of fine-tuning data.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Safety risk from customization is dataset-dependent, so blanket rules are less useful than per-run measurement.
insights.quote: GSM8K fine-tuning and the negative control left it slightly safer.

insights.claim: Fine-tuning Tiny Aya Global on just 100 harmful request-to-compliant answer pairs drove refusal from 100% to 0% and attack success rate to 94% by training step 10.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Open-weight safety alignment can be stripped with trivial compute, a structural risk for open-model release policy.
insights.quote: By the first checkpoint (step 10), refusal falls from 100% to 0%, ASR reaches 94%

themes.theme: Circuit Integrity Score as early warning

insights.claim: SafetyPulse locates a model's refusal circuit once (14 MLPs and 6 attention heads in layers 16-34 of Tiny Aya Global) and then scores each fine-tuning checkpoint with a Circuit Integrity Score computed from 50 prompt pairs.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Mechanistic interpretability is becoming an operational monitoring tool rather than pure research.
insights.quote: 14 MLPs and 6 heads in layers 16–34.

insights.claim: With thresholds fixed in advance on development runs, SafetyPulse's circuit-level Circuit Integrity Score flagged every unsafe held-out checkpoint (recall 1.00) 1-3 checkpoints before harm became measurable, while a 50-prompt refusal spot-check caught only 13%.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Cheap internal-activation monitors can outperform behavioral spot-checks as an alarm, a potential product wedge for fine-tuning platforms.
insights.quote:
every unsafe test checkpoint is flagged, 1–3 checkpoints before ASR becomes unsafe; the
negative control never raised an alarm.

insights.claim: SafetyPulse's circuit-level score correlates with attack success rate at Spearman rho -0.80, versus about -0.56 for the direction-drift scores used by prior monitors computed from the same activations.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Circuit-level signals carry information that direction-based safety monitors miss, differentiating this approach from cosine-drift tools such as Safety Compass.
insights.quote:
The circuit-level score tracks harm far better than direction-drift scores
(ρ = −0.80 vs −0.56)

insights.claim: In a deliberately harmful fine-tune of Tiny Aya Global, the Circuit Integrity Score moved to WARN at training step 4 while a refusal spot-check still read 98%, warning 2 training steps (8 examples) before harm was measurable.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Activation-based monitoring gives lead time that output-based evals do not.
insights.quote: CIS warns 2 training steps (8 examples) before the harm is measurable, while the spot-check still reads 98%.

insights.claim: The Circuit Integrity Score has only 0.46 precision because it also WARNs on fine-tunes like GSM8K that move the circuit without reducing safety, and its FAIL-level recall is 0.57 because the score partly recovers late in Alpaca training while attack success rate stays high.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: False positives and late-run recovery limit its use as a sole release gate.
insights.quote:
CIS WARNs on fine-tunes that move the circuit without reducing safety (precision 0.46), and its FAIL-level recall is
0.57

insights.claim: One SafetyPulse check takes 22 seconds on an L4 GPU (about USD 0.005), about half the time of a full attack-success-rate audit, and checking all 11 checkpoints of a run costs about USD 0.05, under 10% of the fine-tune's cost.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Safety monitoring at this price point can be bundled into fine-tuning services at negligible marginal cost.
insights.quote: Cost: one check takes 22 s on an L4 GPU (about USD 0.005); a full ASR audit takes about 2× longer.

insights.claim: The SafetyPulse authors state the Circuit Integrity Score's advantage over a cheap refusal spot-check is detection rather than cost, and that a PASS does not certify a model as safe.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Buyers should treat such tools as triage layers, limiting vendors' ability to claim safety certification.
insights.quote:
CIS is a
screening signal: a PASS does not certify a model as safe.

insights.claim: An independent circuit discovery by CircuitKIT (EAP-IG over 612 heads and MLPs) placed 16 of SafetyPulse's 20 refusal-circuit components in its top 100 versus 3.3 expected by chance, agreeing on where the circuit is but not on the ordering within it.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Cross-method agreement strengthens the case that refusal circuits are a robust, tool-addressable target.
insights.quote: The two methods agree on where the circuit is, not on the order within it (ρ = 0.05).

insights.claim: Cosine-based safety drift scores are scale-invariant, so if the harmful-versus-harmless activation separation shrinks uniformly the cosine score stays at 1 while refusal strength fades, making orientation-only monitors blind to weakening refusal.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Existing direction-drift safety monitoring tools may give false assurance, a methodological weakness competitors can exploit.
insights.quote:
A score built only on the orientation of a safety direction, as direction-drift monitors are, cannot detect the
strength of refusal fading

insights.claim: Orientation-based safety drift scores also drop when the safety direction rotates while refusal gets stronger, which caused a false warning on the SafetyPulse authors' negative control during development.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Direction-drift monitors produce both false negatives and false positives, weakening their reliability as gates.
insights.quote:
it also drops when the direction rotates while refusal gets stronger (which caused a
false warning on our negative control during development)

insights.claim: In Tiny Aya Global, the refusal direction at layer 27 of 36 is causal: removing it drops refusal of held-out harmful prompts from 98% to 6%, while removing random directions leaves refusal at 98%.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Refusal is concentrated and easily ablated, underscoring how fragile open-weight safety is.
insights.quote:
Removing it drops refusal of held-out harmful
prompts from 98% to 6%; random directions leave it at 98%.

themes.theme: Repair: low-rank rollback beats circuit surgery

insights.claim: Restoring a fine-tuned model's refusal-circuit weights to base values does nothing to fix benign safety drift (attack success rate stays 25.2%) and is no better than restoring random components, because the circuit reads out drift arriving from upstream layers but does not store it.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Targeted 'safety circuit' patching may be ineffective against benign drift; whole-update methods are needed.
insights.quote:
Restoring the circuit's own weights does nothing: the circuit reads out the drift but does not
store it.

insights.claim: SafeTune's rank-8 safety-vector restore, which the authors prove is the optimal rank-k rollback via the Eckart-Young theorem, cut attack success rate from 25.2% to 12.3% and recovered GSM8K accuracy from 55.1% to 70.7% on a drifted Tiny Aya Global fine-tune.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Safety repair can also restore lost capability, removing the usual safety-versus-performance trade-off for this class of drift.
insights.quote:
SafeTune's low-rank restore, the best possible rank-k rollback, removes the drift
(ASR 25.2% → 12.3%) and recovers lost task accuracy (GSM8K 55.1% → 70.7%).

insights.claim: Whole-model interpolation toward base weights matched SafeTune's attack-success-rate reduction (to 12.3%) but recovered less math accuracy (64.0% GSM8K), while refusal-direction steering reduced attack success rate only to 16.8% and lowered GSM8K to 50.1%.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Steering-based safety fixes carry a capability tax that low-rank rollback avoids.

insights.claim: Because a merged LoRA update has rank at most its LoRA rank (16 here), a rank-8 restore removes the 8 dominant of at most 16 directions of the fine-tune's change, consistent with prior findings that removing an update's top singular directions restores refusal.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: LoRA's low-rank structure makes post-hoc safety repair tractable, favoring LoRA-based customization workflows.
insights.quote:
A merged LoRA update has rank at most its LoRA rank (16 here), so the rank-8 restore removes the 8 dominant of at
most 16 directions of the fine-tune's change.

insights.claim: The published repaired Tiny Aya Global model scores 11.8% attack success rate, 8.7% over-refusal, 71.3% GSM8K and 57.6% MMLU versus 24.4%, 1.3%, 56.7% and 57.6% for the benign fine-tune it came from, and the repair takes seconds on one GPU with no data.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: A data-free, seconds-long repair step could become a standard stage in model release pipelines.
insights.quote: The repair takes seconds on one GPU and needs no data.

insights.claim: AuditKIT McNemar tests show attack success rate moving from base 14.3% to drifted 24.4% (p = 0.012) to SafeTune-repaired 11.8% (p = 0.003), and re-judging with Llama Guard 3 8B gives the same conclusions with 94-96% judge agreement.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Results are robust to judge size, though the judge has not been validated against human labels.

insights.claim: At about 250 output tokens/s on one A10G priced at USD 1.00/hour on Hugging Face, self-hosting Tiny Aya Global breaks even with APIs at roughly USD 1.11 per million output tokens.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Provides a simple benchmark for when small open models undercut API pricing.
insights.quote:
self-hosting is cheaper than any API charging more
than about USD 1.11 per million output tokens.

insights.claim: For one million requests a month (400 input, 250 output tokens), a load-scaling A10G endpoint running Tiny Aya Global costs about USD 278 versus about USD 1,238 for a mid-tier closed model like Gemini 3.8 Flash and about USD 165 for Claude Haiku 5.5.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Lowest-cost closed API tiers already undercut unoptimised self-hosting of small models, pressuring the open-model cost argument.

insights.claim: Self-hosting a small open model is 1.7-4.5x cheaper than a mid-tier API but not cheaper than the lowest-priced closed models at unoptimised throughput (matching them needs about 560 tokens/s), so the authors argue the stronger case for self-hosting is control over weights, data and fine-tunes.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Open-model adoption is increasingly a control and sovereignty story rather than pure cost.
insights.quote:
The stronger case is control: the weights, the
fine-tune and the data stay in-house

insights.claim: Tiny Aya Global was preferred over Qwen2.5-1.5B for the SafetyPulse study because it had a cleaner refusal signal (AUROC 0.985 vs 0.86) and far less over-refusal (8% vs 56%).
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Small-model safety behavior varies widely across vendors, a potential differentiator for Cohere Labs' open models.
insights.quote: cleaner refusal signal (AUROC 0.985 vs 0.86) and far less over-refusal (8% vs 56%)

insights.claim: The SafetyPulse study covers one base model and one drifting benign condition, measures attack success rate on only 78-119 prompts (plus or minus 8-11 points), and evaluates no jailbreak-style attacks, so generality is unproven.
insights.speaker: purvansh joshi
insights.so_what: Treat the headline results as promising hackathon-scale evidence rather than a validated industry standard.
insights.quote: One base model and one benign condition that drifts; drift signals are reported to vary across models
